scope_note: 2 Chronicles 1:1 falls outside the Pentateuch and thus beyond the direct scope of J/E/D/P source analysis; the analysis here identifies analogous compositional layers within the Chronistic History (Chr), noting affinities with Deuteronomistic (Dtr) language and the distinctive theological program of the Chronicler (C).

source_units.theological_concerns: Legitimation of Solomonic succession through divine favor; the Chronicler's characteristic concern with the prosperity of the righteous king as a sign of divine approbation; the consolidation formula echoes the Davidic transfer-of-power language.
source_units.structural_markers: The verse functions as a programmatic introduction to the Solomonic narrative in Chr, parallel in structure to the opening of David's reign (1 Chr 11:10; 29:25); the formula וַיהוָה אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ is a Chronistic immanence-formula absent from the Deuteronomistic parallel (1 Kgs 2:12); וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמָעְלָה echoes 1 Chr 29:25 (וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמַעְלָה) almost verbatim, suggesting deliberate Chronistic redactional framing.
source_units.doublet_with: 1 Kings 2:12 (parallel succession notice without the divine-presence formula)
source_units.summary: This verse is best understood as a Chronistic compositional unit — the work of the Chronicler or a close redactor — rather than a document with Pentateuchal source parallels. The combination of the consolidation verb (וַיִּתְחַזֵּק) with the divine-presence formula (וַיהוָה אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ) and the superlative elevation notice (וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמָעְלָה) is uniquely Chronistic and serves a deliberate theological function: grounding Solomon's legitimacy not in palace politics (as in Kings) but in unmediated divine blessing. The divine-name compound YHWH Elohav blends the Tetragrammaton with a possessive relational epithet, a Chronistic stylistic signature that has no direct Pentateuchal source-layer equivalent.

doublets.description: Both verses record the accession of Solomon to the throne of David, but 1 Kgs 2:12 reads simply 'And Solomon sat upon the throne of David his father, and his kingdom was firmly established,' while 2 Chr 1:1 adds the divine-presence formula and the elevation notice, omitting the fratricide and political consolidation narratives present in 1 Kings 1–2.
doublets.significance: The Chronicler's redaction of the Kings source removes morally compromising succession narratives and substitutes a direct theological affirmation of divine favor, revealing the Chr layer's consistent idealization of the Davidic-Solomonic dynasty.

doublets.description: 1 Chr 29:25 uses nearly identical language (וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ יְהוָה עַל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעְלָה) in the context of the assembly's recognition of Solomon, forming an inclusio with the opening of 2 Chr 1.
doublets.significance: The verbal echo between 1 Chr 29:25 and 2 Chr 1:1 is a deliberate Chronistic literary bracket, signaling that the Solomonic narrative is framed by a theology of divinely granted greatness rather than human political agency.

competing_positions.attribution: Wellhausen did not subject Chronicles to Pentateuchal source analysis in the J/E/D/P framework, but in his broader historical-critical work he viewed Chronicles as a late priestly revision of the Samuel-Kings narrative, systematically inserting priestly and Levitical concerns. He would likely identify the divine-presence formula here as priestly-tendency redaction serving cultic legitimation.
competing_positions.note: Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels (1878), ch. on Chronicles as historical source

competing_positions.attribution: Friedman's source work is confined to the Pentateuch; he does not assign J/E/D/P to Chronicles. However, Friedman identifies the Deuteronomistic Historian (Dtr) as responsible for Samuel–Kings and notes that the Chronicler is a distinct, later author who reworked Dtr material. This verse's additions over 1 Kgs 2:12 would be attributed to the Chronicler's distinctive theological hand, not to any Pentateuchal source.
competing_positions.note: Who Wrote the Bible? (1987), ch. 7; The Bible with Sources Revealed (2003), prefatory scope note on post-Pentateuchal books

competing_positions.attribution: Baden's Composition of the Pentateuch restricts its compositional analysis explicitly to Genesis–Deuteronomy and does not address Chronicles. His methodological principle that each source is compositionally independent and complete would suggest treating 2 Chr 1:1 as part of the Chronicler's independent compositional layer, not a redactional seam between Pentateuchal sources.
competing_positions.note: The Composition of the Pentateuch (2012), Introduction, pp. 1–20 (scope definition)

competing_positions.attribution: Japhet, the leading modern commentator on Chronicles, identifies 2 Chr 1:1 as the Chronicler's own composition, not dependent on a direct source beyond the general succession report in Kings; the verse's theology reflects the Chr layer's consistent program of grounding royal legitimacy in YHWH's immediate blessing rather than succession by elimination of rivals.
competing_positions.note: I & II Chronicles: A Commentary (OTL, 1993), pp. 525–527

competing_positions.attribution: Cross's double-redaction theory of Dtr1 and Dtr2 does not directly address Chronicles, which he regarded as a separate post-exilic composition. The presence of YHWH-Elohav compound and the superlative elevation formula in 2 Chr 1:1 would, in his framework, be characteristic of the Chronicler's priestly-Deuteronomistic synthesis rather than either Dtr redaction.
competing_positions.note: Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic (1973), ch. 10

framework_note: Classic Documentary Hypothesis (Wellhausen 1878, Friedman 1987, Baden 2012). Source attribution is analytical evidence, not definitive assignment. The J/E/D/P framework applies strictly to the Pentateuch; Chronicles analysis employs the analogous category of the Chronistic compositional layer (C) and its relationship to the Deuteronomistic History. Scholarly debate is ongoing.
synthesis: 2 Chronicles 1:1 is not analyzable through the classic J/E/D/P Documentary Hypothesis, which is methodologically confined to the Pentateuch; it belongs instead to the compositional layer of the Chronicler, a late post-exilic author working with but significantly revising the Deuteronomistic History. The verse's departures from the parallel in 1 Kings 2:12 — particularly the insertion of the divine-presence formula and the elevation notice — reveal the Chronicler's consistent theological program of legitimating Solomon through unmediated divine favor rather than dynastic violence. The near-verbatim echo of 1 Chr 29:25 confirms that this verse is a deliberate Chronistic redactional bracket, not a seam between independent documentary sources.

bibcrit_hypothesis.title: Chronistic Bracket Frames Solomon via Divine Favor
bibcrit_hypothesis.reasoning: The Chronicler composed 2 Chr 1:1 as an intentional theological revision of the Kings succession notice, suppressing the politically inconvenient fratricide narrative and substituting a direct affirmation of YHWH's presence and gift of greatness. The verbal inclusio with 1 Chr 29:25 suggests a single authorial hand shaping the entire Davidic-Solomonic narrative arc around the theology of divinely conferred rather than humanly seized kingship. This compositional strategy is coherent with the Chronicler's broader program of idealizing the Davidic house for a post-exilic audience seeking models of legitimate, cult-centered governance.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis is methodologically sound in scoping out Chronicles from J/E/D/P, but contains several specific textual and citation claims that need verification or correction.

flagged_claims.reason: 'YHWH Elohav' is not a divine name or 'compound' — it is simply YHWH plus a possessive suffix ('his God'), a common biblical construction, not a 'Chronistic stylistic signature' or distinctive epithet. Treating it as a compound divine name is misleading.

flagged_claims.claim: 1 Chr 29:25 uses nearly identical language (וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ יְהוָה עַל־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעְלָה)
flagged_claims.reason: The MT of 1 Chr 29:25 reads 'וַיְגַדֵּל יְהוָה אֶת־שְׁלֹמֹה לְמַעְלָה לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל'. The Hebrew quotation given is inaccurate.

flagged_claims.claim: וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמָעְלָה echoes 1 Chr 29:25 (וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמַעְלָה) almost verbatim
flagged_claims.reason: 2 Chr 1:1 actually reads 'וַיְגַדְּלֵהוּ לְמָעְלָה' but 1 Chr 29:25 uses 'וַיְגַדֵּל יְהוָה אֶת־שְׁלֹמֹה לְמַעְלָה' — not the suffixed form claimed. The verbal echo exists but the quotation is misrepresented.

Japhet's OTL commentary discussion of 2 Chr 1:1 is in the early 500s page range but the specific page citation 525–527 should be verified; her commentary on 2 Chr 1 begins around p. 524 in the 1993 OTL edition.

Speculative attribution of a position to Cross regarding a verse he did not analyze; framed as 'would, in his framework' but the characterization of Chronicles as 'priestly-Deuteronomistic synthesis' is not a standard Cross formulation.

flagged_claims.claim: the formula וַיהוָה אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ is a Chronistic immanence-formula
flagged_claims.reason: The 'YHWH was with him' formula is widespread across the Hebrew Bible (e.g., Gen 39:2, 1 Sam 18:14, 2 Kgs 18:7) and is not distinctively Chronistic; calling it a 'Chronistic immanence-formula' overstates its source-critical specificity.
